claims.statement: Quartz is an ANN-to-SNN conversion method whose activation representation is time to first spike, with one information-bearing spike per neuron and a balancing or rectifier event. It is not a spike-count or firing-rate code.
claims.scope: Mathematical neural code used by Quartz, distinct from the physical deployment evidence

locators: Section 2, Proposed ANN-to-SNN Conversion Method, pp. 2-4

claims.statement: Quartz was executed on named physical Loihi 1 silicon and reports measured latency, power, energy per inference, and energy-delay product. This is E1 evidence for Quartz itself.
claims.measurement_boundary: NxSDK 1.0.0 on the physical Loihi 1 Nahuku 32 board ncl-ext-ghrd-01. Table 3 separates neuromorphic-core and Lakemont x86 static and dynamic power. The MNIST figures are measured. The paper's preferred CIFAR-10 EDP uses an estimated corrected static-power placement rather than the raw measured placement.
claims.scope: Physical deployment of the proposed Quartz method, not the rate-coded comparison rows

claims.statement: Brehove et al. convert quantized ANNs to sigma-delta neural networks that transmit signed, graded activation deltas. The payload represents changes in activation rather than a firing rate estimated from binary spike counts.
claims.scope: Mathematical and physical event representation of the Brehove et al. conversion

locators: Section 3.1, Conversion and Implementation on Loihi 2, pp. 2-3

claims.statement: Brehove et al. deploy their converted sigma-delta networks on physical Loihi 2 and report accuracy, latency, throughput, power, energy per frame, and energy-delay product. This is E1 evidence for the proposed conversion method.
claims.measurement_boundary: An in-house 16-chip Loihi 2 VPX development board running nxkernel 0.3.0. Loihi activity probes provide chip power and timing. The paper separately reports ordinary I/O and replay-from-on-chip-memory conditions. Host-side input delta generation and output accumulation or decoding remain outside the neurocores. The Jetson comparison uses whole-SoC power and is not boundary-identical.
claims.scope: Physical execution of the proposed ANN-to-SDNN conversion on Loihi 2

claims.statement: Adaptive Fission replaces additional temporal integration with a group of binary neurons carrying unequal fixed weights. Its proposed contribution is a population code layered on existing converted or directly trained SNNs, not unchanged rate coding.
claims.scope: Coding mechanism introduced by Adaptive Fission

claims.statement: Adaptive Fission and its comparison configurations were executed on a physical Lynxi HP201 accelerator. Table 1 reports on-chip memory, time per epoch, and system energy per epoch. This is E1 evidence, with a system-sensor rather than core-only energy boundary.
claims.measurement_boundary: Physical Lynxi HP201 PCIe accelerator, batch size 32. The table reports seconds and watt-hours per evaluation epoch rather than per-sample latency and energy. Energy comes from board sensor readings and includes peripheral circuits, memory, and I/O. Closed interfaces prevent core-only power and operation-count measurement.
claims.scope: Physical deployment of Adaptive Fission and the baselines included in the same hardware table

claims.statement: Adaptive Fission reports unmodified no-Fission QCFS and SRP baseline rows measured on physical Lynxi HP201 silicon. Rate-coded QCFS-lineage networks therefore have reached silicon, although QCFS and SRP did not report these deployments in their own method papers.
claims.measurement_boundary: The same HP201 batch-32, per-epoch, system-sensor boundary used for the Adaptive Fission rows. The rate-coded rows are imported baseline implementations from the original QCFS and SRP codebases. They are not deployments reported by the original QCFS or SRP papers.
claims.scope: Later third-party physical execution of existing QCFS and SRP methods, not evidence that their proposing papers deployed

claims.statement: The standard QuantizeML to CNN2SNN route maps a uniformly quantized integer model to the Akida runtime without a user-exposed multi-timestep firing-rate window. Independent physical-hardware studies describe the converted path as a stepwise quantized ReLU evaluated in one timestep. It must not be classified as ordinary multi-timestep rate coding solely because BrainChip calls the result an SNN.
claims.scope: Observable semantics of the standard converted-CNN route. This does not deny separate temporal or recurrent Akida layer types and does not infer undocumented circuit internals.

locators: QuantizeML user guide, Overview, FixedPoint representation, and Quantization flow, MetaTF 2.19.3
CNN2SNN user guide, Overview and Conversion flow, MetaTF 2.19.3
Ziegler et al., Section III-B.2 and III-C, pp. 4-5

claims.statement: Physical Akida studies report real latency, power, and energy measurements, but they reuse BrainChip's existing QuantizeML and CNN2SNN toolchain rather than introducing a new low-timestep rate-coded ANN-to-SNN conversion algorithm. They therefore do not falsify the narrow paper-level claim.
claims.measurement_boundary: Named physical AKD1000 or Akida PCIe hardware. Individual studies use different boundaries. Ziegler et al. report measured Akida inference and forward-pass latency plus Akida power. Lunghi et al. report device energy per frame and explicitly expose idle-floor power. Putra and Shafique report application-level latency, power, and energy on AKD1000.
claims.scope: Akida as an E1 deployment route and boundary case, not as evidence for a new rate-coded conversion algorithm

locators: Ziegler et al., Table V and Section IV, pp. 6-7
Lunghi et al., Sections 4.1-4.2 and Table 4, pp. 19-21
Putra and Shafique, Sections II-B, III, and IV, pp. 3-8

claims.statement: Through 2026-09-16, the audited corpus and deliberate falsifier search found no paper that both introduces a recent low-timestep, spike-count or firing-rate-coded ANN-to-SNN conversion algorithm and reports that same proposed algorithm on named physical neuromorphic silicon with an on-device measurement. This is a bounded search result, not a universal impossibility claim.
claims.scope: Paper-level, recent low-timestep ANN-to-SNN conversion methods using spike-count or firing-rate representation. It excludes direct-training methods, application papers that reuse an existing converter, classical conversion deployments, non-silicon synthesis, and later third-party baseline deployments.

locators: Section 2 and Section 5, rate-code exclusion reviewed in Audit C
Section 3.1 and Algorithm 1, graded sigma-delta encoding reviewed in Audit C
Sections 3.2 and 4, population-code distinction reviewed in Audit C
Section 2.3.6, reset and rate-coded NxTF route reviewed in Audits B and C
CNN2SNN user guide, Overview and Conversion flow, MetaTF 2.19.3

claims.statement: Andrei et al. extend Few-Spikes conversion to complex-valued layers. The resulting serialized temporal binary code represents values through spike timing and learned temporal coefficients rather than through firing-rate estimation.
claims.scope: Neural code introduced by the complex-valued Few-Spikes conversion

claims.statement: Andrei et al. map their proposed complex-valued Few-Spikes conversion to a physical single-chip SpiNNaker2 board and report board-power measurements. This is E1 evidence for the proposed conversion method.
claims.measurement_boundary: Physical single-chip SpiNNaker2 board. SpiNNcloud software reports board power for the deployed SNN. The comparison target is an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier running the source CNN.
claims.scope: Physical execution of the proposed complex-valued Few-Spikes conversion

claims.statement: Arfa et al. execute a genuine low-timestep rate-coded SNN on SpiNNaker2, but the method uses direct Q-learning and surrogate-gradient fine-tuning rather than ANN-to-SNN conversion.
claims.scope: A direct-training counterexample to broad wording, but not to the narrow conversion claim

claims.statement: Arfa et al. report physical SpiNNaker2 latency, dynamic power, and energy measurements for rate-coded spiking Q-networks run for 10 or 20 ticks. This is E1 evidence for a directly trained low-timestep rate-coded SNN.
claims.measurement_boundary: Physical SpiNNaker2 board executing 8-bit quantized spiking Q-networks. The reported boundary includes inference duration, dynamic power, and energy per episode or inference as defined in the paper, compared with a GTX 1650 GPU.
claims.scope: Physical direct-training deployment, not ANN-to-SNN conversion

claims.statement: When SNN Meets ANN reports PyTorch and Lava-DL accuracy for the proposed low-timestep conversion, but the paper does not establish that the Lava-DL result used a physical neuromorphic backend. The reported accuracy result is therefore E5.
claims.measurement_boundary: Framework-level PyTorch and Lava-DL accuracy comparison. No named chip generation, physical board, profiler, power, latency, or resource measurement is disclosed.
claims.scope: Accuracy evidence for the proposed method, not physical-silicon evidence

claims.statement: When SNN Meets ANN describes a Lava-DL route toward Loihi, but it does not identify the Loihi generation, board, backend configuration, or a physical measurement. The route is E3 rather than physical deployment evidence.
claims.measurement_boundary: Documented Lava-DL route assertion only. Physical execution is unverified and no Loihi generation is identified.
claims.scope: Toolchain path claim kept separate from the E5 accuracy result

locators: Appendix A.10, Deployment of Proposed SNN on Loihi, pp. 22-23
